extracted.intended_audience: diplomats, travelers, and general readers interested in Persian court etiquette and early-19th-century Persian ceremonial practice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural guidance (as reported in a travel/diplomatic narrative) on ceremonial protocol, forms of address, dress, procession, and gift-presentation when receiving an envoy at the Persian court in the early 1800s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astrological timing for entry
rubrics_metrics.description: That, provided the Elchee entered the gate of Teheran at forty-five minutes past two P.M. on the 13th of November, 1800, success would attend his negotiation, and he would accomplish all his wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult an eminent astrologer and follow his prescribed moment for entering the capital. Assign a trusted person with a good chronometer to control pace in the procession so the gate is crossed at the exact appointed minute; the timing is considered crucial to the success of the Mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate dress for presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It was expected he would put on garments suited to the occasion; the meerzâ produced portraits of ambassadors from two centuries ago and proposed that the English envoy adopt the Seffavean ambassador costume as the pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to discuss and, if necessary, negotiate dress requirements. Present historical precedent (paintings/books) when contesting or accepting ceremonial costume; understand local expectations but also assert your representative character if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procession formation and displays of state
rubrics_metrics.description: The marching with fixed bayonets, drawn swords, and trumpets sounding, to the great gate...the infantry part of the escort, with their drum and fifes, and all the Hindustânnee public servants in scarlet and gold, preceded the Elchee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize escorts and military/music display to combine local ceremonial splendour with your own discipline; procession arrangement (who leads, who follows) should reflect both respect for host customs and the envoy's dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating and equality during audience
rubrics_metrics.description: It was agreed...that Sûlimân Khan should make a slight movement, or a half rise, when the Elchee entered the room, and that the latter should seat himself on the carpet on a footing of equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate precise seating and approach rituals to preserve equality of rank. Small physical gestures (half-rise, where to sit) are negotiated details that can signal parity or inferiority—confirm them beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select an appropriate official to meet the envoy
rubrics_metrics.description: There was much and serious discussion as to the rank of the person to be appointed to meet the Elchee at the entrance room...Sûlimân Khan Kajir...was fixed upon to act this part...but it was urged, that the said Sûlimân Khan was of too high rank to rise from his seat to receive any man upon earth, except the king.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the host appoints an official whose rank and expected behaviour match the ceremony's requirements; an official too exalted (or too low) can create protocol problems or unintended slights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate precise forms of address and wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The Persian language is very copious...the word friendship may be expressed by three or four terms, which imply superiority, equality, or inferiority...the terms 'you represented', 'you said', or, 'you commanded'... 'You said' is settled as the term of equality; but 'you commanded' may be frequently interchanged, as tending to show the great respect the parties entertain for each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ skilled secretaries/interpreters to select the exact terms that convey the desired relation (superiority, equality, inferiority). Agree on which phrases denote equality and which connote deference before public exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity rule in politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever one party in the excess of his politeness uses them, the other is to take the earliest opportunity of doing the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the host gives a polite concession (an elevated phrase or gesture), reciprocate promptly to prevent gradual elevation of the other's status and to maintain the agreed balance of dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wording that implies tribute or inferiority when presenting gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: There had been a great desire to give them a name which denoted inferiority of rank...the Elchee would not allow of any such term being used...our presents were termed rarities, and the high rank of the governor-general...was on this occasion upheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on neutral or honorific terminology (e.g., 'rarities' or 'curiosities') rather than 'tribute' or 'offerings' when gifts are announced, to preserve parity between sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical precedent and visual evidence to settle ceremonial points
rubrics_metrics.description: He then produced a parcel; and after opening a number of envelopes, he showed several small pictures of ambassadors who had visited Persia two centuries ago... 'This is the pattern which it is hoped you will adopt, as his majesty desires to follow in all points the usages of the Seffavean kings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputed about ceremony, produce historical examples (paintings, books) that establish precedent for particular dress or procedures; hosts often rely on such precedents to justify requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convene knowledgeable secretaries for fine diplomatic language
rubrics_metrics.description: It was judged necessary to have a congress of meerzâs or secretaries, skilled in such niceties, to settle this important point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble local and envoy secretaries versed in the language's shades of meaning to draft and agree on phrasing for official communications and addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious that small concessions do not elevate local officials' status
rubrics_metrics.description: By giving now and then a term of respect to Hajee Ibrahim, more than he received, the Elchee would add to the consequence of that minister, and not diminish his own... 'they rather alarmed Aga Meer...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid occasional extra deference or language that, when repeated, will raise the perceived status of a local minister relative to the envoy; keep to consistent, agreed protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct during private interviews and public curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: At some [interviews], which were private, he spoke a great deal, and was very inquisitive into the habits and usages of England...The Elchee explained [the English government] as well as he could...The Elchee told the truth, but not the whole truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer the sovereign's questions informatively and diplomatically; tailor truthfulness to the courtly context (omit unnecessarily embarrassing or sensitive details) while preserving honesty and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain composure and use cultural knowledge to avoid faux pas
rubrics_metrics.description: A curious incident occurred as we left the palace. The king's giant...it never entered into his imagination that it was a human being...he passed without taking any notice...he took this to be one. He was first made sensible of his mistake by the praises of his mehmandar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect staged displays intended to elicit reactions; remain composed and draw on familiarity with local iconography or customs to avoid appearing ignorant or surprised. Support from local agents (mehmandar) can explain or smooth over misunderstandings.
